item.title: What's new in Pyr: week of November 9
item.dc:creator: Nurro
item.description: Every update to Pyr from November 9 to 15, 2026, newest first.
item.content:encoded:
Everything that changed in Pyr this week, newest day first. A new day is added each afternoon, with the Today in Pyr note in your bell.

Wednesday, November 11#

Pyr now has Cilia Quest Training, a guided tutorial for marking cilia that earns the Cilia Signal Achievement. You can also redo the edit in the Merge and Cut tutorials, and the chat online count now matches.

Cilia Quest Training: Use the Training button in the Quests tab to practice marking a cilium and its centrioles, then earn the Cilia Signal Achievement.

Redo Merge and Cut edits: Going back to the start of the Merge or Cut tutorial now resets the cell, so you can make the edit again.

Chat online count fixed: The online count and name list in chat now match, you show online as soon as you write, and long links wrap.

Smoother tutorials: The Get Started, Merge and Cut tutorials have clearer boxes and steadier tips, and partial cuts now explain how to finish.

All 8 updates#

  • Who is online, fixed. The online count in chat and its list of names now always match, and anyone around in the last 5 minutes counts as online. Writing in chat now shows you online right away, even with Pyr open in several tabs. Chat no longer gets a sideways scroll bar; long words and links wrap instead.
  • A Cilia Quest tutorial. New: a Cilia Quest tutorial. Start it with the Tutorial button in the Quests tab, or from the menu under Quests. It shows a cell the lab has already marked, then you mark the cilium and its two centrioles yourself and get checked as you go. It ends with a short quiz on choosing a status, and finishing it earns the Cilia Signal Achievement. Leaving the Merge or Cut tutorial for another one no longer leaves merge mode or its messages behind. A tutorial box that takes a moment to load now shows a loading card.
  • Cilia Quest Training. The new Cilia Quest tutorial is now called Cilia Quest Training, and its button in the Quests tab reads Training. The first time you open Cilia Quests, the training starts by itself if you have not done a quest yet. Close it with the ✕ if you already know how.
  • Get Started: the split screen box. In Get Started, the 2D EM tab now glows when the box points to it, and pressing SPACE no longer skips the box before you finish reading. Click Next when you are ready. The electron microscope boxes show one yellow point, and the images always open flat in their normal orientation.
  • Cut tutorial fixes. The Cut tutorial always uses its own two cells. If you try it again right away, it waits a moment while they are put back, so you always get the 2D cut too. The first boxes of the Cut tutorial open closer in on the cut. Help me tips stay on screen instead of vanishing after a moment. If a cut takes off only part of the merger, the box changes to tell you what is left and how to finish it. The box before the 2D cut says more clearly what comes next.
  • Tutorial touch ups. Get Started: the box about finding the continuation shows one hint point, and it no longer flickers away. Merge tutorial: the How to Merge box sits lower so it no longer covers the top bar, and the Merge icon glows until merge mode is on. Merge tutorial: the first merge opens closer in, and the tips on the last merge box show as a bulleted list again.
  • Going back in the Merge and Cut tutorials. If you go back to the start of the Merge or Cut tutorial after making the edit, the cell is put back to how it began, so the yellow piece returns and you can do it again.
  • Cilia Quest Training touch ups. The steps for drawing the cilium line now sit in the box where you draw it. A new tip in the daughter centriole box explains how to tell it apart from the basal body. The status box links to Celia's Cilia Status Guide, with real examples of each status.

Players made 794 edits and completed 13 cells.

Tuesday, November 10#

Today brings small polish: the tour's portal now swirls with twice as many sparks, and the Help me button in tutorials and sandboxes reads Hide help once help is open.

All 9 updates#

  • Number pad and layer 10 keys. The number pad picks layers just like the number keys above the letters. Ctrl + 0 opens layers 10 and up, the next one each time you press it. In the blog editor, pasting into a picture caption keeps the words in the caption, and a link copied from a list stays a link.
  • BC Challenge on the Retina. On the Retina, the Available tab is now BC Challenge: every cell left to map there is a bipolar cell. The Retina instructions are now How to map a bipolar cell.
  • Faster big views. Views with hundreds of cells kept in folders, or many annotation points, draw and respond faster. Cell status is looked up for many cells at once, so long segment lists fill in their marks sooner. If the lab's server can't be reached, a cell just cut or merged shows "couldn't check" and is asked again, instead of looking unproofread.
  • Smoother scrolling and highlighting. The annotation list no longer freezes while you scroll it. Highlight ignores a click that misses the cell, such as one on the dataset's outline box, instead of putting marks in empty space. Long segment lists look up marks for 50 cells at a time.
  • Faster with thousands of annotations. Views with thousands of annotation points stay smoother while you pan and zoom. The Retina question fits a small window, so its Save button is always in reach. The box drawing tool that could appear by accident is gone. Admin notifications no longer jump back to the top while you add players.
  • Alt+click finds the cell. Alt+click on a cell finds it in your list, even over a highlight point or annotation, and no longer opens Highlight or moves the mark.
  • A brighter portal. The tour's portal swirls with twice as many sparks, spiraling in from the rim to its glowing core. The Starship and its contrails now come out of the middle of the portal and stay in front of the ring, even when you replay the flight.
  • Cheer on achievements. You can react to a player's achievement in chat with an emoji, a quick way to say congratulations. The Update ready button has an i beside it, so you can still read what changed after pressing Later.
  • Help me becomes Hide help. In the tutorials and sandboxes, once help is open the Help me button reads Hide help, so it is clear how to close it.

Players made 477 edits and completed 14 cells.

Monday, November 9#

Retina cells you claim now open with a Highlight layer, a new tour of Pyr lets you fly the Axon Runner into a real neuron, and Get Started shows a neuron being traced.

Retina cells open with Highlight: Claimed Retina cells open with one Checked Highlight layer, and you can still add annotation layers from the Cell Library or Settings.

Fly the new tour: Press the rocket by the chat box to fly the Axon Runner into a real neuron, then explore a Martinotti cell in MICrONS.

The tour on phones: On a phone the tour fills the screen, a lightning button sends pulses, and buttons step through the Martinotti cell's partners.

Watch a neuron get traced: Get Started page 2 shows a brain block being sliced and imaged, then a traced branch growing into a whole 3D neuron.

Smaller changes: Today in Pyr in chat has an Open button, Settings can stop cells turning by themselves, and Ctrl+Z brings back a closed layer.

All 16 updates#

  • From a block of brain to a neuron. Page 2 of Get Started now shows how a connectome is made with real data: a tiny block of brain is sliced, each slice is imaged, and a whole neuron is reconstructed in 3D.
  • Open Today in Pyr from chat. Nurro's Today in Pyr line in chat has an Open button that brings up the full report.
  • Start playing in the Sandbox. Once you have finished Merge and Cut, the Sandbox card says Start playing. It takes you to a Sandbox cell of your own to proofread, with a short note on what to do.
  • Get Started page 2, shorter. Page 2 of Get Started no longer sends you to Connectome 101, since the Starship tour now explains what a connectome is.
  • Watch a neuron get traced. On page 2 of Get Started, the tiny block of brain now sits on one of the neuron's branches. You see the AI color in every cell, then the traced branch lights up and grows into the whole neuron.
  • Try the new tour of Pyr. A rocket by the chat box opens a prototype of the new tour that new players will see: a Starship flies into a real neuron and shows you its parts, its synapses and an action potential. From its last screen you can explore a much bigger neuron in MICrONS and visit the cells it connects to, or start Get Started from the beginning. Settings has a new switch under 3D looks, Turn cells slowly, to stop the view turning by itself. It is still a prototype, so please send ideas and problems with a bug report.
  • Tour touch ups. The tour's message boxes draw their glowing frame at the right size, including the Leave the introduction question. Start the tour shows a loading screen while your first neuron arrives, instead of a black screen. A stray line under the tour invitation is gone. The X on the Leave the introduction question now closes the tour.
  • A cleaner neuron view. The neuron animation on Get Started page 2 no longer draws lines across the volume behind the cell.
  • A smoother tour of Pyr. The tour's ship is now called the Axon Runner, and it flies smooth banked curves: up the apical dendrite, two barrel rolls on its dive to the axon, and nose first everywhere. A new launch screen shows while your first neuron loads, with a warp jump into the cell. The Axon Runner's holograms build up out of its beam once it has stopped, and the tour's panel follows. In MICrONS the Axon Runner scans the Martinotti cell's synapses with a hologram bar, shows its stats as a hologram, and counts its partners: 5,195 cells it hears from and 3,660 it sends to, with the cell types it hears from and sends to most. Visiting a partner cell, the Axon Runner swoops up through the synapses the two cells share, and each one lights with a burst of sparks. The welcome now says Pyr is pronounced peer, and the X closes the tour from the Leave question. Turning the cell no longer drags the parked Axon Runner around.
  • The Axon Runner's banked swoop. On its way to the side of the view the Axon Runner swoops out and away, rolls onto its side through a banked turn, and comes back toward you. It always shows its back as it flies, stays in view as it climbs the dendrite, and parks closer to the soma. The orange downstream cell grows out from the synapse and is named in the tour, and the connectome step fills the volume with dozens of other cells. The Axon Runner's hologram beam is a soft triangle of light.
  • The tour on phones. On a phone the tour now has the whole screen: the top and bottom bars step aside while it runs, also in MICrONS. Holograms on phones are short and easy to read, and the cell no longer turns on its own. The Axon Runner swings out beside the cell before it turns, never through it, and hovers clear of the branches at the soma. A yellow lightning button on the action potential step sends another pulse with each tap. In MICrONS on a phone, Upstream cell and Downstream cell buttons step through the Martinotti cell's partners one at a time. The portal on the way into MICrONS stays a modest size, and the welcome and action potential words are shorter.
  • A smoother flight to the neuron. In the tour, the Starship now flies a clean curve from the soma out to its spot beside the neuron, and stays easy to see while the view pulls back. The rocket key always starts a fresh flight, even if the last one never finished.
  • Retina cells open with Highlight. A Retina cell you claim now opens with one Checked Highlight layer and the Highlight box ready, instead of five annotation layers. Prefer annotations? Press + Annotation layers on your cell in the Cell Library, or turn them on for every Retina claim in Settings, under Jumping and views. Your Checked marks stay in one Checked layer, with no more Checked 1 and Checked 2. Claiming a cell takes you to My Cells, with your new cell in view. Click your current cell's row in the Cell Library to open Complete. Your cell stays at the top while the form is open, so nothing is cut off. A layer tab has one close button, an x, and Ctrl+Z brings a closed layer back. For neuroglancer's two buttons (hide to the side panel, and delete), turn on Classic layer tab buttons in Settings, under Neuroglancer. How to map a cell, in the Cell Library, opens in a box of its own with a picture of a bipolar cell. The outline around the volume is a softer blue. If you have worked on Retina cells, Pyr asks you once whether they open with Highlight or with the annotation layers. Cilia Quests always open with their annotations.
  • Clearer messages when a cell cannot be marked. When marking a cell done does not work, the message now says plainly what went wrong, and shows the whole cell IDs when the crosshairs are in the wrong cell.
  • Log out, Not now, and tour fixes. Log out is now the last option in the menu at the top right. The last Get Started box has a Not now button, so you can finish without starting the Merge tutorial. The Starship tour and the tutorial boxes no longer show at the same time. In Get Started, the box about the big black empty space now shows the black space in the 2D image. A bug report still sends when your view cannot be saved, with your position instead.
  • A better bug report. What you write in a bug report is kept until you send it or press Clear, and clicking outside the box no longer closes it. Set up the screen first: the report steps aside so you can open what the picture should show, then press Take screenshot. The details box has bold, italics, bullets and numbers.

Players made 1,167 edits and completed 21 cells.

item.title: How Do We See? The Mysteries Hiding in Plain Sight
item.dc:creator: Amy R. Sterling
item.description: Some of the biggest mysteries of vision begin in a thin layer of cells at the back of your eye. Here is the known, the unknown and how you can help map the brain to make neuroscience history.
item.content:encoded:
Every time you open your eyes, billions of photons enter your pupils. A fraction of a second later, you're seeing the world in color, depth, and motion. You can recognize a face across a crowded room, follow a bird in flight, or notice something moving at the edge of your vision.

How does your brain accomplish all this?

Surprisingly, scientists are still figuring it out. And some of the biggest mysteries begin in a thin layer of cells at the back of your eye.

Your retina is a little piece of brain#

Light enters your eye through the cornea and pupil. The lens focuses it onto the retina, a delicate sheet of neural tissue lining the back of the eye.

Here, specialized cells called rods and cones detect light and convert it into electrical signals. Those signals pass through an intricate network of neurons before traveling along the optic nerve to the brain.

But the retina does much more than detect light. It helps identify edges, changes in brightness, and movement. Some retinal neurons even respond preferentially when objects move in a particular direction.

Your eyes are already making sense of the world before your brain gets the message.

A forest of neurons#

The retina contains many different kinds of neurons, arranged in layers. Bipolar cells relay information from photoreceptors, amacrine cells shape and modify those signals, and ganglion cells carry the results to the brain.

Their shapes are extraordinary. Some stretch vertically between layers, while others extend elaborate branches sideways, gathering information from their neighbors.

The arrangement of these branches matters. Which cells connect, where they connect, and how strongly they communicate all help determine what information reaches the brain.

What don't we know?#

Quite a lot, actually.

Scientists are still working to identify all the different types of retinal neurons and understand what each contributes to vision. We know some of the circuitry responsible for detecting motion, contrast, and changes in light, but we don't yet understand how all those circuits work together when we look at a complex, constantly changing world.

And there's an especially tantalizing question: If we could map every neuron and every connection in the retina, could we predict what the circuit sees?

A wiring diagram alone isn't enough. Neurons are living, dynamic cells. But combining their anatomy with recordings of their activity will bring us to many new discoveries. That possibility is what makes modern connectomics so exciting.

A million tiny clues#

With advances in electron microscopy and artificial intelligence, scientists can now reconstruct neurons in extraordinary detail.

Pyr is one such prjoject. It includes several connectomics datasets, including Eyewire II, a volume of mouse retina containing ~100,000cells. For hundreds of its neurons, researchers have both detailed anatomy and recordings of how the cells respond to visual stimuli.

That gives us a rare opportunity to connect the shape of a neuron with what it actually does. And there are countless connections left to investigate.

Help us discover what's hiding in the retina#

Mapping neural circuits is painstaking work. AI can trace neurons through microscopic images, but it makes mistakes. Human eyes are remarkably good at spotting where a branch has gone astray.

That's where you come in.

In Pyr, the new citizen science game from the creators of Eyewire, players help map real neurons from neuroscience datasets, including the EyeWire II retina.

Every correction contributes to a more accurate map. And every better map gives scientists new opportunities to investigate how neural circuits work.

We can't promise what discoveries lie ahead. Perhaps we'll uncover clues about how we see or make progress toward solving issues of the eye such as blindness. One thing is for certain: this is uncharted territory, and mapping it is only possible with your help!

That's the lovely thing about exploring the unknown: you don't get to know what you'll find before you begin.

Come explore the brain with us. Play Pyr and help unravel the mysteries of vision!

Play Pyr

item.title: Guide to Mapping Bipolar Cells (BCs)
item.dc:creator: Amy R. Sterling
item.description: Every image you see passes through a bipolar cell. Learn what these relay cells do and how to proofread one in Pyr.
item.content:encoded:
Every image you have ever seen passed through a bipolar cell. These small and tidy cells sit in the middle of the retina. In Eyewire II/ Pyr's retina dataset, they are some of the cells you will encounter most frequently. Here is what they do and how to proofread one.

What bipolar cells do#

Light hits the photoreceptors (the rods and cones) at the back of the retina. The photoreceptors can't talk to the brain directly. They hand their signal to bipolar cells, and the bipolar cells pass it on to both amacrine and ganglion cells. Ganglion axons form the optic nerve and send a pre-processed signal carrying information about objects and movement from the eye to the brain.

Bipolar cells are a critical relay step, and the direct path from photoreceptor to neuron.

Bipolar cells are also part of EyeWire history. EyeWire players reconstructed bipolar cells and the starburst amacrine cells they connect to. The work showed that bipolar types with different timing connect to different parts of the starburst cell, a wiring pattern that helps the retina tell which way something is moving, which became the first ever Eyewire publication in the prestigious journal Nature back in 2014 (Kim et al., Nature).

Today, Eyewire II players are carrying that work forward, and you have already mapped more than 10,000 cells together:

Every bipolar cell you proofread in Pyr adds to that map. If you'd like to learn more about the science, scroll to the bottom of the post. Below find instructions on how to proofread Bipolar Cells (BCs).

Claiming a BC#

  1. Head to the Retina Dataset (if you don't have access yet, see this post).
  2. Open the Cell Library, navigate to Available Cells, and Claim one.
  3. Proofread the cell (instructions below)
  4. When you have fully proofread the BC, mark it Complete

How to proofread a BC#

Check the whole cell, branch by branch:

  • Dendrites: follow each one up to its tip. Look for pieces that broke off (they need a merge) and pieces of other cells stuck on (they need a cut).
  • Axon: follow it down to the terminals, and check that the terminals all belong to this cell.
  • Each branch end: a bipolar cell has many small ends. Check every one.

Keep track of what you checked#

A bipolar cell has lots of small branch ends, and for proofreading accuracy you must mark each one as you finish it. You may use Highlight OR Annotations. Or both if you're crazy. Use whichever tool you like best. The only annotation that is required is "Can't Complete", which should be used to mark any spots on the branches that cannot be traced due to issues like EM image quality.

Highlight Mode

  • Turn on Highlight Mode from its icon in the top bar.
  • Ctrl+click two points on the cell, and the stretch between them is marked with a highlighter stroke.
  • To soma marks the way from a point back to the cell body, and the button beside it marks every branch beyond a point.
  • Pick a color, or add your own, and press Undo if you mark the wrong piece.

Annotations

  • Make an annotation layer and pick the point tool.
  • Ctrl+click to drop a point on each branch end you have checked.
  • Change the layer's color and point size so your points are easy to see.
  • Points are listed in the layer's panel: right click one to jump to it, or step through them with the arrows.

Some people like Highlight because it colors the branch itself. Others like annotation points because they can step through them one by one later. Either way, when every end is marked, you know the cell is done and you can mark it complete and claim another. If you get stuck, you can ask for help in Chat or via the Help feature in the Cell Library.

Happy proofreading, and thank you for helping map the brain!

More Science!#

Check out the cast of the retina here.

Each bipolar cell has two ends, which is where the name comes from:

  • Dendrites reach up to the photoreceptors and collect their signal.
  • An axon runs down into the inner retina and ends in a spray of axon terminals, where it passes the signal on.

Why they matter#

Bipolar cells don't just pass the picture along. They split it up.

  • ON and OFF. Some bipolar cells respond when light gets brighter (ON), others when it gets darker (OFF). In the mouse, types 1 to 4 are OFF, and types 5 to 9 and the rod bipolar cell are ON.
  • About 15 types. Each type reports a different piece of the scene: fast or slow changes, light or dark, fine detail or broad strokes. The rod bipolar cell carries vision in dim light.
  • Layers. Each type ends its axon at its own depth in the inner retina, so the signals stay sorted into separate channels, like wires in a cable.

These parallel channels are the raw material for everything the retina computes before the brain sees anything. So if you think about it, your BCs are helping to map BCs and uncovering how mammalian eyes see. Pretty cool!

item.title: Mapping MEC
item.dc:creator: Amy R. Sterling
item.description: The lab needs help proofreading axons!
item.content:encoded:
The lab needs help proofreading axons!#

Here is how:

  1. Claim a cell

Open the Cell Library on MEC, click Available, pick a cell and press Claim. It is yours until you complete or release it.

  1. Find the AIS

The AIS (axon initial segment) is where the axon leaves the cell body. It is the starting line for everything else.

Under your cell in the Cell Library, open Marks and pick AIS. Press Go to the lab’s AIS point. The lab has already placed a point where they believe the axon starts. Check it. The axon usually leaves the soma (or a thick dendrite close to it) as a single smooth, thin branch with no spines. If the lab’s point is on it, good. If it is off, move the crosshairs onto the start of the axon. Press Confirm AIS here. The AIS mark goes where the crosshairs are.

If the cell has no distinct axon, skip the mark and say so in your notes when you complete it.

  1. Proofread the axon (and only the axon)

Follow the axon from the AIS out to every one of its ends. Along the way, fix what is wrong.

  • Missing pieces: the branch stops in 3D but clearly goes on in the image. Find the next piece and merge it on (press M, then Ctrl+click both pieces).
  • Something that does not belong: a piece of another cell joined on. Cut it off (press C, Ctrl+click red points on one side of the join and blue points on the other, then press Submit cut).

You may cut the axon off from the rest of the cell during proofreading. Just make sure to merge is back before you complete the cell.

Leave the rest of the cell alone. There is no need to fix or check dendrites, spines and the cell body. We're investigating the downstream partners of these cells, which are reached through synapses on the axons, so that's why we need these first.

Do not merge mitochondria. Inside the axon you will see small dark ovals, often as separate pieces <image>. They are mitochondria, the powerhouse of the cell. We plan to analyze them later, so please keep their meshes separate.

Some axons run out past the edge of the imaged volume. Proofread up to the edge and move on.

Stuck on a branch? If a branch should go on but you cannot find the next piece, ask for help in the Cell Library or in chat. You can share your view and carry on in other areas until you hear back.

Keeping track. On a big axon it is easy to lose your place. Highlight (Shift+H) lets you colour the stretches you have already checked. You can also use Lantern mode to hide sections of the cell so that you can focus on specific branches.

The other annotation layer in Marks (True End, Can’t Fix and Hits Edge) are optional now. Use them if they help you keep track, but only the AIS is required.

  1. Complete it

When every end of the axon is done, Complete the cell, either in the Cell Library or with the Δ button next to its segment ID, and choose Axon complete. It counts as one of your completed cells, and the lab’s spreadsheet records it. Proofread axons count toward you cell completion, even if eventually we go back and add more to the dendritic arbor.

Merge Errors#

MEC is currently experiencing some errors with splits and merges. This is a dataset error rather than an issue with the game interface.

For now please follow this protocol: If you encounter errors please add new annotation layers named "Merge Errors" and "Split Errors" and use the line annotation type to mark where you want the split or merge. You can then continue to complete the rest of the cell as normal. Please leave a note that you encountered errors and what type (merge, split, both) when you submit the cell as complete.

Need help?

Use chat, ask in the Help tab, or drop us an email.

Need a bigger challenge? Try Super Quests :)

Thank you for mapping neurons in Pyr. Every axon you finish goes straight into the connectome, bringing us one branch closer to understanding the brain. For science!

item.title: Super Quests: MEC Inhibitory Interneurons
item.dc:creator: Amy R. Sterling
item.description:
Some neurons ask for an afternoon. These could keep you exploring for weeks.
We’re introducing Super Quests in Pyr: a chance to help map enormous inhibitory interneurons in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC), a brain region involved in navigation and memory.
These cells have sprawling branches…
item.content:encoded:
Some neurons ask for an afternoon. These could keep you exploring for weeks.

We’re introducing Super Quests in Pyr: a chance to help map enormous inhibitory interneurons in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC), a brain region involved in navigation and memory.

The medial entorhinal cortex helps the brain keep track of where you are. It is home to grid cells, which fire in a regular pattern as an animal moves through space. Interneurons are the cells that hold that activity in check: they inhibit their neighbors, and the giant ones reach a great many of them.

The new Super Quest features giant interneurons of the MEC. Each has so many branches that it can take weeks to finish. Nobody has mapped these cell types before. You can be among the first to see one whole and help us decipher what they do!

A precise question: who do they inhibit?

The lab has selected 29 cells and grouped them by their predicted targets:

  • Pyramidal Target — 17 cells: predicted to inhibit pyramidal neurons exclusively.
  • Non-Pyramidal Target — 12 cells: predicted to inhibit non-pyramidal cells exclusively.

Those are predictions. Your proofreading will help us reconstruct these neurons and analyze their connections to find out whether the predictions hold.

How a Super Quest works#

Open the Cell Library on MEC and pick the Super Quests chip. You may claim one at a time and keep it for up to two months (if you need longer, just message us). A Super Quest sits beside your other claims and does not count against them.

Marks. Mark the AIS, where the axon leaves the cell; it is the one mark that is required. Others are optional. You could use True End for a branch that stops naturally, and Checked for a place you have looked at and found right, so you know where you have been. Hide marks clears them from the view when you want to see the cell itself. We are working on Highlight mode in MEC. For now, annotations highlight the immediately surrounding area on a cell, so you can add lots of annotations to effectively highlight a branch.

Your time is counted. This is how the lab learns how long these cells really take and will help us estimate the amount of time required for proofreading in this and future datasets. Pyr adds up your active time on the cell and shows it on the row, such as 14 h 20 min so far. It counts only while the cell is on screen, Pyr is the tab in front, and you have used the mouse or keys in the last 5 minutes. There is no need to hurry. It is most important to map the cells accurately.

"Save view" keeps your layers and marks with the claim, and the claim keeps the cell's ID through every merge and split.

A special achievement is waiting for anyone who accurately completes a Super Quest. Prefer something lighter? Try mapping MEC pyramidal axons. Guaranteed only moderately difficult!

Thank you for contributing to neuroscience!

item.title: How to unlock Edit access in Pyr
item.dc:creator: Amy R. Sterling
item.description: Practice in the Sandbox, then show us ten edits you would make, right inside Pyr. Here is how the access check works, what happens after you send, and where to find help while you learn.
item.content:encoded:
The Sandbox is where everyone starts in Pyr. Every signed in player can cut and merge there, and nothing you do in it touches real science. Once those tools feel natural, you can ask for edit access so that you can edit real neurons and help map the brain.

Getting started#

Everything you need to learn lives in the menu at the top right of Pyr (the burger icon).

  • Site Tour. A quick walk around the screen: the top bar, the views and where everything is.
  • Tutorials. Take them in order. Get Started shows you how to move around a cell in 3D and step through the electron microscope images. Advanced Interface covers layers, coordinates, annotations and settings. Merge and Cut teach the two edits on practice cells, so a slip costs nothing.
  • Merger Sandbox. Practice cells, each with a merger to find and cut. The menu keeps count of how many you have done.
  • Utilize Chat if you have questions, or ask for help in the Cell Library (neuron icon in the top bar).

What we ask for#

Before you can contribute to real science, you must demonstrate that you know your way around a neuron. For this, submit test edits on cells in the sandbox or on the Retina dataset where you found mergers or missed extensions. 10 demo edits are currently required:

  • Seven cuts. Find places where two cells were wrongly joined. Place red and blue Multicut (cut) points on each side of where you would cut.
  • Three merges. Find places where one cell was wrongly broken in two. Press M, then Ctrl+click the two pieces to place merge points.

Place the points, but do not submit the edit. Leave each mistake in place, so we can see it the way you found it.

How to request Edit access#

  • Open the menu at the top right and choose Ask for retina access, at the very bottom.
  • Place your cut or merge points, then press Save this view as cut 1 (or merge 1). Pyr keeps the view, every point you placed, and a note if you want to add one. The points are cleared afterwards, so the next one starts fresh.
  • Click any saved example to fly back to it, or press Replace to swap in a better one.
  • On a laptop, press Slim to make the box small while you work.
  • When all ten are saved, press Send for review.

What happens next#

Someone from the team looks at every example and every point you placed and you will hear back in your notifications.

If your edits look right, your edit access is granted and the world of connectomics opens to you. If a few need another look, we mark them and tell you why. Redo those and send again.

Taking more than one try is normal. You are never locked out and there is no limit on tries. If you have practiced in the Sandbox for two weeks and still feel unsure, reach out to us. We are happy to help.

Help while you learn#

  • The tutorials in Pyr. After Get Started, open the menu at the top right and take Merge, Cut and Advanced Interface.
  • Chat and the Cell Library. Ask in chat, or ask for help on a cell from the Cell Library (the neuron icon in the top bar).
  • Videos. How to merge, how to split, and Find Path, which helps you trace a merger back to where it starts. There is also a full playlist of advanced tutorials. We are working on tutorials using the new Pyr interface.
  • The Proofreading Guide.
  • Chat

Once you are in, you are part of the team building new maps of the brain. For science!

item.title: The Cilia Quest: a new way to help in Pyr
item.dc:creator: Amy R. Sterling
item.description: Quests are a new kind of task in Pyr. Your challenge, should you choose to accept it, is to find and tag the primary cilium on starburst cells in the retina, without ever having to proofread the cell.
item.content:encoded:
Calling all Pyr players! there's a new Quest on the horizon, and we need your help!

We're on the hunt for primary cilia, important cellular appendages that receive and process environmental signals. Cilia serve as “antennas” that cells use to sense the chemistry of their environment. Each cell only has one primary cilium, will you be the one to find it?

How to Hunt for Cilia#

  1. Open the Cell Library and click Quests. If you are on another dataset, press Switch to Retina.
  2. Press Claim on an available cell. The cell and it's annotation layers will open on screen. Each cell in a Cilia Quest is retinal neuron. Somewhere on its cell body there may be a cilium, a thin appendage that projects from. This is what we quest for.
  3. Find the cilium (if there is one). At its base sits the basal body, and close by is a second structure, the daughter centriole. Mark all 3 structures, if present.
  4. Put the crosshairs inside the cell and press Submit.
  5. Choose a cilium status from the list. Don't know which to choose? Select your guess to see help text below. Or check out this post for a full explanation of all statuses with examples!
  6. Select whether the cilium was "split" - part of all of the cilium was not attached, or "merged" - cilium was fully visible in the original segmentation. If no cilium was present, make no selection.
  7. Add a note if needed, and press the 2nd Submit button!

You can hold three cells at a time. Release sends a cell back for someone else.

About each structure:

  • Cilium - a columnar structure that projects from the cell's soma. Microtubules should be visible inside (greyish lines).
  • Basal body - a centriole at the base of cilium. It's always inside to the soma membrane. When no cilium is present, there may still be a basal body.
  • Daughter centriole - A second centriole. It is often found near, but not attached to the basal body. In some cases it can be very far from the BB -- keep scrolling!

Important note! Some cells have no visible cilium, but often you will still be able to locate the two centrioles inside the soma.

annotating the structures#

To annotate a cilium, you'll need to use the 3 annotation layers. Click a layer to select it.

  • Polyline annotation - use this to annotate the cilium centerline. Once selected, Ctrl and click along the cilium, then press Enter. Backspace removes the last point and Esc cancels the line.
  • Point annotation - use this to annotate the basal body (BB) and daughter centriole (DC). CTRL + click to place it. Always double check your layer when placing!

Putting it all together#

Here's an example of a cell with a cilium that's been fully annotated and is ready to complete!

Dive Deeper#

  • Check out the lab's scientific guide to cilia with tips on how to locate them.
  • Watch an in-depth training video.
  • Here's quick guide to each cilia status and when to use it. Click the image to enlarge, and the link to see an interactive example.

Other statuses:

  • Need Help - You can't find any cilium or centrioles, or there's another issue that stops you from annotating the cell. Good to leave clarifying notes in most cases!
  • No cilium - Nothing found. This should only be used after review (use Need Help if you are the first annotator)

Where your answer goes#

When you submit, your status, your notes and a link to your view go to the lab, with your name and the date. Pyr celebrates with you and tells you how many annotations you placed on that cell and how many Quests you have completed. Your profile keeps the count.

Tell us how it goes#

The Cilia Quest is our very first Quest! If something is unclear or could work better, ask in chat or send a report with the feedback button.

item.title: Achievements in Pyr: how the steps work
item.dc:creator: Amy R. Sterling
item.description: Overview of achievement tiers in Pyr.
item.content:encoded:
Pyr has two sets of Achievements you earn just by doing science. One counts the cells you complete. The other counts the edits you make.

Achievements you earned before the November 2026 update stay yours, in the Legacy Achievements row of your Trophy Case.

Below find a list of the thresholds.

Cell Completion Achievements#

Every cell you complete counts.

  • Your first cell earns your first Achievement.
  • Then 5, 10, 15 and 20 cells.
  • Then 30, 40, 50, 75, 100, 125 and 150 cells.
  • Every 50 cells up to 500.
  • Every 100 cells up to 2,000.
  • Every 250 cells up to 5,000.
  • Every 500 cells up to 10,000.
  • After 10,000, Every 1,000 cells.

Editor Achievements#

Every merge and every split counts as an edit.

  • Your first edit earns your first Achievement.
  • Then 10, 25, 50 and 100 edits.
  • Every 100 edits up to 500.
  • Then 750 and 1,000 edits.
  • Every 500 edits up to 5,000.
  • Every 1,000 edits up to 20,000.
  • Every 2,500 edits up to 50,000.
  • Every 5,000 edits up to 100,000.
  • After 100,000, every 25,000 edits.

What will you unlock next?#

Open your Trophy Case to see the ones you hold and how far you are from the next one.

Thank you for helping to map the brain. For science!

item.title: Upgrades to chat
item.dc:creator: Amy R. Sterling
item.description: Chat in Pyr has a set of new tools. Search the conversation, add bold and underline, see where new messages begin, and find your own messages at a glance.
item.content:encoded:
Chat is where a lot of Pyr happens: questions about a tricky branch, a link to a cell, a cheer when someone finishes a big one or earns a new achievement. This week it picked up a set of expansions suggested by Krzysztof Kruk. Bonus: None of them takes up any more of your screen.

Bold and underline#

There is no toolbar to learn. Put a star, *, on each side of the words you want in bold. Put an underscore on each side of the words you want underlined, like _this_.

Or select some text in the message box and press Ctrl+B for bold or Ctrl+U for underline. Press it again to take the mark off. You can use both on the same words.

The marks only count around a whole word or phrase. A name with an underscore in it, or a sum written with stars, stays exactly as you typed it.

Search the conversation#

Click the magnifier at the top of the chat. The line where you type a message becomes a search line, and the chat shows only the messages that match.

  • Type one or more words. A message has to contain all of them.
  • Put a minus sign in front of a word to leave out messages that have it, like merge -queue.
  • Put words in quotes to find them together, like "cut off".
  • Type from: and a name to see one player's messages, like from:Nseraf.
  • Search one day with on:10/8, or a stretch of days with after:yesterday and before:2026-10-01. The words today and yesterday work too.

Click any result to jump to that message in the conversation, with everything around it. Press Esc, or click the magnifier again, to go back to chat.

Search looks through the messages chat has loaded. To reach further back, press Search earlier messages too at the top of the list to include the past 14 days. When you search for a day, chat brings in the earlier messages by itself.

Find your own messages#

A thin bar now appears to the left of your own messages, making them easy to spot. If you would rather not see it, open Settings and switch off Mark my own messages in chat.

See what is new#

When you open Pyr, or come back to it from another tab, a line across the chat shows where the messages you have not seen begin. It reads New since you left. Everything below it is new. The line goes away once you send a message.

Pinned messages#

Sometimes there is one thing everyone should see, like a dataset opening or an event starting. The Pyr team can now pin a message to the top of chat. It sits in one line above the conversation. Click it to jump to the message, or press the small x to hide it for yourself.

Thank you, Krzysztof#

Search, bold and underline, and marking your own messages all came from one player's suggestions. If you have an idea for Pyr, send it in with the feedback button. For science!

item.title: Highlight mode: color in what you have checked
item.dc:creator: Amy R. Sterling
item.description: A new tool for keeping track of your work on a big cell. Mark a stretch of a branch and its surface takes a color, so you can see what is done and what is left.
item.content:encoded:
Proofreading a big cell means checking a lot of branches, and it is easy to lose track of which ones you have already been down. Until now the usual trick was to drop a point at the end of each branch. That marks a place. It does not show you the stretch of cell you checked.

Highlight mode does. You pick two points on a cell, and the stretch between them takes a color. The cell fills in as you work, and whatever is still plain is what is left to do.

How to use it#

  1. Click the spray can in the toolbar to open Highlight.
  2. Hold Ctrl and click the cell where your checked stretch starts. On a Mac, hold Cmd. Holding H and clicking works too.
  3. Turn and move the view as much as you like.
  4. Hold Ctrl and click where the stretch ends.

The game finds the path along the cell between your two clicks and colors the surface of the cell along it.

Pick your colors#

Highlight starts with three colors: Checked, Needs a look and Problem. Click a color's swatch to change it. Use + Add to make your own, with any name you like, up to eight colors in all.

Your colors are saved to your account, so they are there on any computer you sign in on.

Color reach#

The Color reach slider sets how far out from the middle of the branch the color spreads, from 0.5 to 8 µm.

Here is the same stretch of dendrite at two settings. At 2.5 µm the color covers the shaft, but the tips of the longer spines stay the cell's own purple.

At 4 µm the color reaches all the way to the spine tips.

A wider reach covers thick branches and their spines. A narrower reach keeps the color off neighboring branches that run close by. You can move the slider after you have made your marks, and they all update.

Good to know#

  • Undo removes your last mark. Clear all removes every mark.
  • Your marks are saved with your view. They come back with the autosave, with Save view on a claim, and in a link you share.
  • Marks stay put when you merge or split. They are attached to the place, so editing the cell does not lose them.
  • Long paths can take a while. If the game cannot find the path within a minute it stops, and nothing is marked. There is also a Stop tracing button.
  • You can drag the Highlight box anywhere on the screen, and it stays where you put it.
  • Highlight is not on every dataset yet. Where it is off, the spray can is greyed out.

Tell us how it goes#

Highlight is new, and it will change as you use it. If something does not color the way you expect, send it with the feedback button in the game, or tell us on the forum.

item.title: Write your own scripts for EyeWire II
item.dc:creator: Amy and the EyeWire team
item.description: EyeWire II now has a small set of tools for player scripts, plus a guide to get you started with Tampermonkey. Also this week: split screen replaces the 4 panel view, your view saves itself, and the fly nerve cord joins the dataset list.
item.content:encoded:
Players of the original EyeWire built some of its best features themselves. Bigger annotation dots, extra statistics, faster ways to get around: many of them started as a script one player wrote for their own browser and then shared.

EyeWire II now supports that properly. There is a guide for getting started, and a small set of tools made for scripts to use.

What a script is#

A script is a small piece of code that changes the game on your computer only. It runs through Tampermonkey, a free browser extension. Nobody else sees your script, and you do not need permission to write one.

What scripts can use#

Until now a script had to reach into the inner workings of the game, which change with almost every update. So scripts broke often. The new tools are the parts we promise to keep working:

  • Your cells and your view. The cells you have selected, the cell under the crosshairs, your claims, and where you are looking.
  • Events. Run your code when you claim, release or complete a cell, when your selection changes, or when you switch datasets.
  • A button and a panel. Add your own button to the top bar and your own side panel.
  • Annotation layers. Make a layer of your own and add points and lines to it.
  • Settings. Save your script's settings in your browser.

Everything else is still open. Scripts can reach the viewer directly for anything the tools do not cover.

Open the scripts guide

The guide has setup steps, the full list of tools, and six example scripts you can copy.

A word on safety#

A script runs as you. It can do anything you can do in the game, including editing cells with your sign in. Scripts you write yourself are fine. Before you install a script from someone else, read it, or ask in chat whether others use it. Scripts are made by players and are not reviewed by the EyeWire team.

Tell us what is missing#

We asked the script writers on the forum what they need, and the answer was that scripts grow out of whatever rough edge someone notices that week. So the list of tools starts small on purpose. If your script needs something that is not there, ask on the forum and we will add it.

Also new this week#

  • Split screen replaces the 4 panel view. Press Space to flip between split screen and the single panel under your mouse. Nothing lands you in 4 panel any more.
  • Your view saves itself. Annotations, layers and position are saved to your account as you work. Open the game on any computer and it offers to pick up where you left off.
  • Save view on a claim. In the Cell Library, the cell you are working on has a Save view button, so your annotations stay with the cell.
  • The fly brain and nerve cord. BANC is now in the dataset switcher, and the three MICrONS versions share one card.
  • Claim several cells at once. The Cell Library can fill your claims from the Available list in one click.
  • A faster Cell Library. Your own cells load first, and long lists draw 200 rows at a time.
